title: Generative AI: Language, Recommendations and Verification
status: Draft practice questions; teacher review required
instructions: Open practice based on the published course and lab. Local scores are not official grades.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes real language-model tokens?
options: Each token is always exactly one English word
Tokens may represent whole words, parts of words, punctuation or other units
A token is always one pixel
A token is a verified fact
questions.explanation: Tokenisation maps input text to a sequence of units. Our on-page splitter is a deliberately simplified demonstration.

questions.prompt: The classroom toy splits 'AI can help students!' into which sequence?
options: AI, can, help, students, !
One token containing the entire sentence
One token per letter, always
Five numeric probabilities, with no text units
questions.explanation: In the lesson's simplified representation punctuation is separated from the words; this is not a claim about a real GPT tokenizer.

questions.prompt: A toy model assigns 60% to 'blue' after 'Today the sky looks ...'. What does that mean?
options: The sky is certainly blue right now
The model has checked the weather
'blue' is the highest-scoring illustrated continuation among the three given choices
A 60% chance that all model-generated sentences are true
questions.explanation: The displayed numbers are illustrative candidate preferences, not verified statements about the world.

questions.prompt: A toy recommender has 5 science clicks and 2 music clicks. Which topic ranks first?
options: Science
Music
They always tie
The system needs pupil names to decide
questions.explanation: In this teaching example the larger click count ranks ahead.

questions.prompt: Why is a single click an incomplete measure of someone's preference?
options: Clicks are always random
A person may click because of curiosity, surprise or disagreement
Clicks contain the entire person's biography
A click guarantees the content is accurate
questions.explanation: An interaction is evidence of behaviour; motives are not known from that signal alone.

questions.prompt: A newsletter says 80% voted yes. The tally is 12 yes and 8 no. What percentage is correct?
Which is the independent evidence for the newsletter vote claim?
options: How fluent the AI wording sounds
The original anonymous tally of yes and no
The model's confidence in its own wording
The length of the generated sentence
questions.explanation: Compare the claim with the actual original count, not a generated paraphrase.

questions.prompt: Which actions are appropriate when using AI-assisted writing? Select ALL.
options: Review and correct important factual claims before publishing
Paste classmates' passwords to provide context
Use anonymous or invented data in classroom examples
Publish an AI draft without reading it
questions.explanation: Verification and minimal-data handling are part of a responsible workflow.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a text suggestion from an authorised automated action?
options: Any generated sentence automatically grants permission to publish
A tool-using program must have explicit permission to perform its action
A chatbot message is identical to a sent email
Checking permissions makes code unable to run
questions.explanation: Generating a suggested message is not the same as being authorised to send or publish it.

questions.prompt: Which statements follow from the Week 10 exercises? Select ALL.
options: Our tokenizer and feed ranker are classroom demonstrations, not real platform implementations
The largest next-word score is not proof that the sentence is true
Real GPT models always use the exact split from the demo
A persuasive claim needs no independent evidence
questions.explanation: Do not conflate illustrative toy systems with operational production models or treat plausibility as truth.
